orders.description: Appeal from the June 26, 2015 order denying the landlord's summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice in the parking lot outside her workplace. Defendant owned the premises and leased them to her employer.

legal_issues.finding: The out-of-possession landlord established no duty to remove snow or ice; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of a statutory, contractual or assumed duty.
Defendant established its out-of-possession status and entitlement to summary judgment; a reserved right of entry alone did not impose a repair duty.
The court considered a duty imposed by statute or regulation and found no triable issue on that basis. No particular provision or proven violation is identified.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted proof of out-of-possession status; the opinion does not specify the form of that proof.

quality.notes: Workplace subtype and exact accident date are not stated. A third-party action appears in the caption but the appealed ruling substantively resolves plaintiff's claim against the landlord.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on ice in the parking lot outside her workplace. The premises were owned by the defendant and were leased to the plaintiff's employer.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Lane, J.), dated June 26, 2015, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting proof that it was an out-of-possession landlord and, thus, had no duty to perform repairs or remove snow and ice from the premises

In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise [*2] a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendant had a duty to remove snow or ice under statute or regulation, the terms of the lease, or a course of conduct
A landlord's reservation of the right to enter property to inspect and make repairs does not in itself give rise to a duty to make repairs
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Appeal from the July 10, 2015 order denying defendant's summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: After swimming and showering at defendant's club, plaintiff testified that he slipped on water after stepping from matting onto the locker-room tile floor. He also described recurring water from a shower and staff use of towels near a carpeted locker area.

legal_issues.finding: The majority rejected the proposition that water anywhere in the locker room is necessarily incidental to its use and therefore precludes negligence liability.
The majority left the notice question unresolved as a matter of law; it did not conclusively find actual notice.
Missing evidence of the last inspection/mopping and the possible duration of water accumulation precluded summary judgment on constructive notice.
The majority considered recurring shower-water overflow and staff use of towels as support for an inference of insufficient mopping; it did not conclusively establish notice of a recurring condition.
In the dissent only, the judges reasoned that they could reach the necessarily-incidental-water argument even if defendant had not raised it. This is not identified as the majority's holding.
The majority found the existence of a hazardous wet condition unresolved and distinguished pool/shower precedents. The dissent would reverse; the controlling disposition is affirmance.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's deposition described swimming, showering and slipping on water.
Maintenance employee and supervisor testimony described customary mopping, warning signs and the inability to establish the last mopping.
Maintenance staff kept no logs/checklists; no written mopping schedule or confirmation was identified. Missing records were not proof of safe conditions.

quality.notes: The text establishes defendant's club operations, maintenance and fee-paying members, but does not expressly identify private ownership or a lease; a private operator alone is insufficient under the current codebook. Retain review/property_unclear pending human application of the private-control rule. The majority affirmed; P008–P011 are a dissent and E013/E014 describe dissent reasoning, not controlling holdings. E014 is not coded as a current-disposition cue. P011 also explicitly references the majority's affirmance. Exact accident date and plaintiff's membership/visitor status are unstated.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Lucindo Suarez, J.), entered July 10, 2015, which denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, affirmed, without costs.

Plaintiff asserts that he slipped and fell on water on the tile floor of defendant's men's locker room. He testified at deposition that after swimming in defendant's pool and then showering in the poolside showers, he walked down the corridor between the pool and the men's locker room.
The locker room also has two separate locker areas, one for daily users, the other for annual fee-paying members; the latter locker area is carpeted.

Defendant's maintenance supervisor, Kendrick Bonner, testified that defendant's maintenance staff did not keep logs or checklists of work performed, and that they always kept "wet floor" signs in the area of the locker room at issue, so that the patrons would exercise care and so that the maintenance staff would not have to mop the area as often.

We are unable to determine as a matter of law, on this record, whether a hazardous or defective condition was created by the presence of water at the location at issue on defendant's locker room floor, and, if so, whether defendant had notice of it.

Plaintiff asserted that at times, one of the shower stalls would cause a water problem in which water flowed into the central locker room corridor and soaked the carpeting at the entrance to the so-called annual members' locker room; staff would periodically place towels on the floor in front of the entrance to the annual members' locker room to protect the carpet.
The submitted evidence precludes determination as a matter of law regarding whether defendant had constructive notice of a hazardous wet condition.

In particular, in the testimony of defendants' witness Eddie Vega, although he asserted that the floor was mopped "maybe every 15 to 20 minutes," he also acknowledged that there was no written schedule or written confirmation of mopping performed, and he was unable to affirmatively state when or whether the area in question had been mopped that day.

Furthermore, plaintiff's assertion that maintenance staff used towels at the doorway to the members' locker room to prevent that room's carpet from getting wet provides further support for the inference that staff did not mop up water on the main locker room tile floor with sufficient frequency to keep hazardous conditions from developing.

Finally, since plaintiff was swimming for 40 minutes before returning to the locker room and slipping, the water could have accumulated at that spot and remained there for long enough to justify an inference of constructive notice.
Accordingly, the submissions failed to establish that defendant had a right to judgment as a matter of law.

Neither of those holdings stands for the broader proposition that any water on a tiled floor anywhere in a locker room must preclude a claim for negligence because water is "necessarily incidental" to the entire locker room's intended use.
To the extent defendant failed to raise this point, we may nonetheless reach it because it is apparent from the face of the record and could not have been avoided had it been timely raised
Accordingly, I would reverse the order denying defendant that relief, and respectfully dissent from the majority's affirmance of that order.

To establish a defendant's liability in a slip and fall case, a plaintiff must show that the plaintiff's injury was caused by a hazardous condition on the defendant's premises of which the defendant had actual or constructive notice

orders.description: Appeal from the July 1, 2015 order denying defendant's summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Decedent allegedly tripped on a rug while entering defendant's store. The rug had been placed flat over a recessed mat system, and the opinion describes her foot catching its front edge.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant placed the rug, but established that its placement did not create a dangerous or defective condition; the opposing expert's placement theory was insufficient.
The court identified decedent's foot picking up the rug's edge as the mechanism and found no evidence that a rug defect or slipping rug caused the fall.
Plaintiff's expert affidavit was speculative and conclusory; an examination approximately '2V2 years' later, as rendered in the source, did not establish the condition at the accident time.
Defendant established that the entrance rug was not dangerous or defective, and plaintiff failed to produce sufficient contrary evidence.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted decedent's deposition testimony, including her observation that she saw nothing wrong with the rug before falling.
Photographs of the rug were among defendant's submissions supporting the description of its flat placement.
Plaintiff submitted an expert affidavit criticizing rug placement; the court rejected it as speculative/conclusory and temporally insufficient.
A video of the incident submitted in opposition showed a trip over the front edge. The opinion does not specify the recording equipment or operator.

quality.notes: Private retail premises/control is supported by defendant's store and its placement of the entrance rug; title ownership and decedent's customer/visitor role are not inferred. The source's '2V2' and other OCR typography are preserved in quotations; the accident date is unstated. Hazard category describes the alleged rug obstruction, not a finding that it was dangerous.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is granted and the complaint is dismissed.
Memorandum: In this action, plaintiff seeks damages for injuries sustained by Joan M. Slattery (decedent) when she allegedly tripped and fell on a rug entering defendant’s store.

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (John L. Michalski, A.J.), entered July 1, 2015 in a personal injury action. The order denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by showing that the rug it placed in the entranceway to the store did not constitute a dangerous or defective condition

Defendant’s submissions, which included the deposition testimony of decedent and photographs of the rug, established that the rug had been laid flat over a “recessed mat system” at the entrance to the store, and decedent did not see anything wrong with the rug before she fell
Those submissions established that decedent simply tripped over the rug, not because of a defect or irregularity in the rug, but because her foot picked up the edge of the rug
We agree with defendant that the affidavit of plaintiff’s expert is speculative and conclusory

In his affidavit, the expert opined that the placement of the rug over the recessed mat system caused a tripping hazard inasmuch as the rug was “not designed to be used over another carpet or the recessed mat system but on a flat, level and flush floor.”

Although the rug may not have been designed to be placed over another rug or the recessed mat system, the video of the incident, which was submitted in opposition to the motion, shows that decedent tripped over the front edge of the rug. There is no indication that the rug slipped, and there is no record evidence that the rug constituted a defective or dangerous condition at the time of the fall.

We note in any event that the affidavit of plaintiffs expert was based on his examination of the area where decedent fell approximately 2V2 years after the accident and thus is insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact with respect to the condition of that area at the time of decedent’s fall
We agree with defendant that Supreme Court erred in denying its motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Appeal from the November 22, 2017 order denying defendants' summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against them.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a walkway on defendants' property. Deposition testimony described snow removal before the accident and potentially inadequate salting of the walkway.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the landowner's snow-and-ice duty, including the reasonable period after a storm ends.
A triable issue remained whether defendants created the slippery condition.
A triable issue remained whether defendants had actual notice; actual notice was not conclusively established.
A triable issue remained whether defendants had constructive notice; constructive notice was not conclusively established.
Defendants' own submissions raised a triable issue whether the storm had sufficiently abated; the doctrine did not establish entitlement to summary judgment.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted deposition testimony about snow accumulation, removal efforts and salting. The opinion does not identify the deponents.

quality.notes: Premises subtype, plaintiff's role and exact accident date are not stated. Snow-removal testimony raised factual issues rather than establishing negligence.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this premises liability action seeking damages for injuries he allegedly sustained when he slipped on a walkway on property owned by defendants-appellants (defendants).
The order, among other things, denied the motion of defendants General Motors Corporation and GM Powertrain for summary judgment.
Contrary to their contention, defendants failed to establish their entitlement to summary judgment based on the storm in progress doctrine.

Here, defendants' own submissions, which included deposition testimony establishing that snow removal efforts had been underway for more than an hour prior to plaintiff's accident and that only a negligible amount of snow had accumulated in the three hours prior to the accident, raise a triable issue of material fact whether the storm had sufficiently abated to preclude application of the doctrine

Further, defendants submitted deposition testimony establishing that, prior to plaintiff's accident, workers were removing snow in the area of the walkway where plaintiff fell and should have salted that walkway, but may not have adequately done so.
Thus, triable issues of fact exist whether defendants created or had actual or constructive notice of the slippery condition
It is well settled that "[a] landowner is not responsible for a failure to remove snow and ice until a reasonable time has elapsed after cessation of the storm"
We affirm.

orders.description: Appeal from the June 6, 2019 order, limited to the branch denying summary judgment on negligent snow/ice removal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the branch of defendant's motion seeking dismissal of the negligent snow/ice-removal cause of action.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while descending a service entrance stairway on defendant's property. He and his wife alleged negligent removal of snow or ice from the stairway.

legal_issues.finding: A property owner electing to remove snow during an ongoing storm must exercise reasonable care.
Defendant failed to show that its snow-removal efforts neither created nor exacerbated the hazard. The court did not conclusively find that defendant created it.
The court addressed the storm-in-progress framework and the duty to avoid creating or worsening a hazard when voluntarily removing snow during a storm.

quality.notes: Affirmed insofar as appealed from is a full affirmance of the appealed branch, not a mixed disposition. Premises subtype and plaintiff's role are unstated. The opinion does not identify specific evidence types supporting the snow-removal submissions.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff Edwin Coreano (hereinafter the plaintiff) allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell while walking down a service entrance stairway located at certain property owned by the defendant.

The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the cause of action alleging that the defendant negligently removed snow and/or ice from the subject stairway.
If a storm is ongoing, and a property owner elects to remove snow, it must do so with reasonable care or it could be held liable for creating or exacerbating a natural hazard created by the storm

Here, the defendant failed to make a prima facie showing that the snow removal efforts it undertook neither created nor exacerbated the allegedly hazardous condition which caused the plaintiff to fall

Since the [*2] defendant failed to meet its burden, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the cause of action alleging that the defendant negligently removed snow and/or ice from the stairway, without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiffs' opposition papers
The plaintiff, and his wife suing derivatively, commenced the instant action alleging, inter alia, that the defendant negligently removed snow and/or ice from the subject stairway.
